doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Race on the New York scene then and now
summary: Nussbaum says early New York bands were mixed and people listened with ears, and that it is still about the music.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I mean when I first came to New York I was playing with just a broad cross section of everybody on a racial basis. And it wasn’t about what you looked like it was like if you could play, you had the desire, you had the love, and you were giving to the music. And people were listening with their ears, not with their eyes.

I think it’s probably the same way. I’m sure that I don’t worry about it. I just don’t worry about it. It’s like if a guy wants to hire me I’m there for the music. I go in, I try to do the best I can for what the situation warrants. Hopefully when people hire me they trust me to bring forth what I can do. And I’m there for the good of the music. And I try to get along with everybody, there we go again, Kum-ba-ya baby, that’s what you want. That’s what it’s all supposed to be. You know music is supposed to be a thing where we all get together and all that other stuff is not supposed to interfere. It may all affect the way people think about stuff and their viewpoints, but when you get on the bandstand man, the music, it tells you what to do. That’s the common denominator. And we’re all supposed to work together for that. I mean that’s the bottom line.
